title: Undoing Changes
tagline: Git almost never deletes anything -- "undo" usually means "point somewhere else", which is why it's recoverable.

concept.label: What
concept.text: git restore undoes working-directory/staged changes; git revert undoes a commit by adding a new one; git reset moves a branch pointer.

concept.label: Why
concept.text: Mistakes are certain -- a committed secret, a broken commit, an accidental file. Each needs a DIFFERENT undo tool.

concept.label: How
concept.text: Revert is safe for shared history (adds a new commit); reset rewrites history (fine locally, risky if already pushed).

concept.label: When
concept.text: restore: before committing. revert: after committing and pushing. reset: after committing, NOT yet pushed.

concept.label: Where
concept.text: Every real project eventually needs all three -- knowing which one matters more than knowing the syntax.

mnemonic.label: R.R.R.
mnemonic.text: Restore (uncommitted) -> Revert (safe undo, shared) -> Reset (rewrite, local only)

sandboxNote.text: practice these on a throwaway branch or repo first -- reset in particular can discard work if used carelessly, which is exactly why this module exists.

code:
echo "oops" >> README.md
git restore README.md            # RESTORE: discard this uncommitted change entirely

git add README.md && git commit -m "Bad commit"
git revert HEAD                  # REVERT: adds a NEW commit that undoes the last one
git log --oneline                # notice: both commits are still in history, visible

git add README.md && git commit -m "Another bad commit"
git reset --soft HEAD~1          # RESET: undo the commit, keep changes staged
git reset --hard HEAD~1          # RESET: undo the commit AND discard the changes -- careful

git reflog                        # the safety net: EVERY position HEAD has ever been at,
                                   # even ones reset --hard just "deleted"

cycle.title: Read the concept table once
cycle.text: The decision that matters most: has this been pushed and shared? If yes, revert (adds history, safe for collaborators). If no, reset is fine (rewrites history, only affects you).

cycle.title: Type the code yourself — no copy-paste
cycle.text: Do all three on a throwaway branch. Then deliberately run reset --hard on a commit, panic slightly, and use git reflog to find and recover it -- that recovery IS the lesson.
cycle.hint: git reflog is the closest thing Git has to an undo-for-your-undo. Nearly everything feels unrecoverable right up until you check it.

cycle.title: Apply it to your own data
cycle.text: Intentionally commit something you don't want (a debug file, a typo commit message) to a real repo, then fix it with the correct tool for whether you've pushed it yet or not.

cycle.title: Reflect & note
cycle.text: Did you use reflog for real? What did its output look like, and did it actually get you back to where you wanted?
cycle.placeholder: e.g. reflog showed a list like 'a1b2c3d HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~1' -- I ran git reset --hard a1b2c3d using that hash and got my 'lost' commit back completely intact...

cycle.title: Tick off before moving on
checklist: I can explain when to use restore vs revert vs reset.
I used git restore to discard an uncommitted change.
I used git revert and confirmed the original commit stayed visible in history.
I deliberately lost a commit with reset --hard and recovered it with reflog.
I wrote a reflection note above.
